title: Thread-Safety Fundamentals for Objects
summary: What it precisely means for a class to be thread-safe, why race conditions happen, and why a class can look safe method-by-method yet still break under concurrent use.

slides.markdown:
A class is **thread-safe** if it behaves correctly when multiple threads call it at the same time, with no extra coordination from the caller. Most bugs here aren't crashes — they're silent, wrong answers: a counter that loses increments, a list that ends up shorter than expected.

Think of a shared class like a single whiteboard two people are handed markers for at once — without a rule for who writes when, sentences interleave into nonsense. This topic builds the vocabulary — race conditions, critical sections, compound operations — you need before you can design or defend a thread-safe class in an interview.

A class is **thread-safe** if, when multiple threads call its methods concurrently — in any interleaving, with no extra synchronization from the caller — it still produces correct results and never corrupts its own internal state.

The precise part matters: thread-safety isn't about "usually works" or "hasn't crashed yet." It's a guarantee about *every* possible interleaving, including ones your tests never happened to hit. A class that's correct for 999 out of 1000 thread schedules is not thread-safe — it's a bug waiting for load.

The corollary: thread-safety is a property of the class's contract, not of any one run. You prove it by reasoning about shared mutable state, not by running it under load and seeing no failures.

slides.sectionTitle: Race conditions: mutating shared state without ordering
slides.markdown:
A **race condition** happens when the correctness of a result depends on the timing of two or more threads, and at least one of them writes to shared state. Both threads read a value, both compute based on what they read, and whichever writes last "wins" — silently overwriting the other's work.

Take a shared `int total` that two threads both increment. Each increment is really three steps — read `total`, add 1, write it back. If both threads read `total = 5` before either writes, they both compute `6` and write `6` — one increment is lost, and `total` is now 6 instead of the correct 7.

Races don't need bad luck to trigger — under real load, with many threads and many operations, they happen constantly. They just don't show up in a single-threaded test run.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: an interleaving that corrupts a counter's state
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: timeline diagram with two vertical thread lanes (Thread A, Thread B) both operating on a shared counter starting at 5; each lane shows three steps -- read total (5), compute total+1 (6), write 6 -- with Thread B's read happening between Thread A's read and write, so both threads write 6 and one increment is lost, ending value 6 instead of the correct 7 >>>

This is the exact interleaving from the previous slide, drawn out step by step. Thread A reads `5`, then before it writes back, Thread B also reads `5` — both threads computed their new value from the *same* stale read.

The bug isn't in either thread's logic; each one's three steps are individually correct. The bug is that "read, compute, write" isn't a single atomic step, so the scheduler is free to interleave another thread's read in the middle of it.

slides.sectionTitle: Critical sections: code that must run one thread at a time
slides.markdown:
A **critical section** is the span of code that touches shared mutable state and must not be interleaved between threads — it has to run to completion in one thread before another thread can enter it. In the counter example, "read total, add 1, write total" is the entire critical section.

Identifying the critical section precisely is the actual design skill here. Too narrow — say, protecting only the write — and the read-compute-write sequence can still interleave, so the race survives. Too broad — wrapping unrelated work in the same lock — and you serialize work that never needed to be serial, killing throughput for no safety benefit.

The rule of thumb: a critical section is exactly the smallest span where "some other thread could see or change this state mid-operation" would produce a wrong answer.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: an unsafe Counter and why it breaks
slides.subTitle: Java example

slides.markdown:
Not every non-thread-safe class is broken by design — some are documented as **safe only if the caller synchronizes externally**, pushing the responsibility outward instead of solving it internally.

| | Thread-safe class | Caller-must-synchronize class |
|---|---|---|
| Who guarantees correctness | The class itself, internally | Whoever calls it, externally |
| Caller's burden | None -- call any method from any thread | Must wrap every access in the same lock |
| Example | `ConcurrentHashMap` | Plain `HashMap`, `ArrayList` |
| Failure mode if caller forgets | N/A | Silent corruption, no exception |

**How to decide:** if a class will be shared across threads you don't control (a library, a cache used by unrelated callers), make it internally thread-safe — you can't rely on every caller remembering to lock correctly.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: each method looks safe, but the class isn't
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Every method in this class only does one simple thing, so the class must be thread-safe."

**Why it's wrong:** thread-safety is about *compound* operations, not individual method bodies. A class can have perfectly correct individual methods and still be unsafe if calling code combines two calls (a read then a write) in a way that assumes nothing changes in between — the classic `if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)` "check-then-act" pattern is unsafe even if both `containsKey` and `put` are individually safe.

**Correct model:** ask not "is each method safe alone?" but "is every sequence of calls a caller might realistically make still correct under interleaving?" Thread-safety is a property of the whole usage pattern, not a per-method checkbox.

slides.sectionTitle: Interview framing: what "design a thread-safe X" really checks
slides.markdown:
When an interviewer says "make this class thread-safe," they're rarely grading whether you can type the `synchronized` keyword. They're checking whether you can **name the exact race** — which field, which operation, which interleaving — before reaching for a fix.

Strong answers narrate: "here's the shared mutable state, here's the read-modify-write that isn't atomic, here's the smallest span I need to protect." Weak answers jump straight to "I'll synchronize the whole class" without ever naming what could go wrong without it — which reads as pattern-matching, not understanding.

The follow-up question is almost always "does your fix hurt throughput, and could you do less?" — so hold your first answer loosely and expect to defend the trade-off.
